Hey everyone, I’m Safa, the maker of buddylist 👋

Remember MSN Messenger? I built buddylist to bring that feeling to working with coding agents.

Add Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and OpenCode as buddies. Bring them into a group chat, ask Claude to build a feature, then have Codex review it. They share the conversation’s project folder. You can also choose another agent to continue an unfinished checklist. [...] Separate contacts can work in their own Git worktrees. Chat tabs and forked chats share the existing folder. Review diffs, run a terminal, preview your app and manage PRs beside the conversation. There are retro themes, nudges and winks too.

buddylist is free for macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows and Linux, with optional Buy Me a Coffee support. Bring your own agent accounts; provider access and usage are separate.

3) Semantic Transformation Layer (Refactoring APIs)

Replace edit-text loops with safe deterministic operations:

- `RenameSymbol()`  
- `ChangeSignature()`  
- `ExtractInterface()`  
- `MoveModule()`

This is where reliability jumps and token cost collapses.

4) Organization Memory Layer

Structured engineering memory with retrieval:

- ADRs / RFCs linked to code  
- invariants (“never change this field directly”)  
- incident learnings  
- approved patterns (“safe approach”)  
- ownership boundaries

Not chat history.

Actual institutional knowledge that agents can consult _and verify_.

5) AI-native SDLC Orchestrator

Ticket in → shipped fix out: [...] But it’s still a retrofit.

### Retrofit tooling vs AI-native tooling (the distinction that matters)

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Image 5

Right now, we’re still in the retrofit era.

We bolt AI agents onto tools designed for humans:

- IDEs  
- search  
- LSP  
- CI pipelines  
- debuggers

Helpful? Absolutely.   
Optimal? Not even close.

Retrofit tooling asks:

> “How do we make existing tools smarter?”

AI-native tooling asks:

> “What primitives do agents actually need to operate software systems safely?”

That’s a very different question.

And the answer isn’t another chat sidebar.

### What AI-native developer tools actually look like

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Image 6 [...] This is how agents stop “reading codebases”…

…and start operating software systems.

### The endgame isn’t “AI inside IDE” — it’s AI-native SDLC

The final product isn’t autocomplete on steroids.

It’s an AI-native development lifecycle:

> ticket → research → patch → tests → PR → rollout

With guardrails built in:

- policies   
- observability  
- staged rollouts  
- rollback plans  
- ownership constraints

In this world:

- PRs become verification artifacts (not “please review my work”)  
- CI becomes enforcement (not a polite suggestion)  
- IDE becomes just one interface — like a terminal

The core becomes an agent-first system that understands code, executes experiments, validates outcomes, and ships changes safely.
